text: Melting ice requires about 334 kilojoules per kilogram (latent heat of fusion)
as_written: Ice needs about 334 kilojoules to melt each kilogram
source: Standard physical constant for water, e.g. NIST Chemistry WebBook / CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics

text: Earth's ice totals roughly 30 million cubic kilometers (Antarctica about 27 million, Greenland about 2.9 million, glaciers about 0.16 million)
as_written: roughly 30 million cubic kilometers
source: Bedmap2 (Fretwell et al. 2013, The Cryosphere); BedMachine Greenland (Morlighem et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters); Farinotti et al. 2019, Nature Geoscience

text: Melting that ice needs about nine trillion trillion joules (derived: volume x ice density 917 kg/m3 x 334 kJ/kg)
as_written: around nine trillion trillion joules
source: Author's calculation from the volume sources above and the latent heat of fusion

text: Earth intercepts about 170 quadrillion watts of sunlight (solar constant 1361 W/m2 times Earth's cross-section)
as_written: about 170 quadrillion watts
source: NASA / SORCE Total Irradiance Monitor solar constant; calculation with Earth's radius

text: Melting all the ice would take about a year and a half of all sunlight striking Earth (derived)
as_written: for a year and a half
source: Author's calculation from the two figures above

text: Antarctic ice is about two kilometers thick on average and over four kilometers thick in places
as_written: about two kilometers thick on average, and more than four kilometers thick in places
source: Bedmap2, Fretwell et al. 2013, The Cryosphere

text: Antarctica holds about 90 percent of the planet's ice
as_written: around ninety percent of all the ice on the planet
source: US National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)

text: Long shallow wave speed equals the square root of gravity times depth; for 2 km depth this is about 140 m/s, about 500 km/h (derived)
as_written: about 140 meters per second ... roughly 500 kilometers an hour
source: Shallow-water wave theory, standard fluid dynamics; calculation with g = 9.8 m/s2

text: Coldest air temperature measured on Earth is minus 89.2 C at Vostok Station
as_written: minus 89.2 degrees Celsius, at Vostok Station
source: World Meteorological Organization Archive of Weather and Climate Extremes

text: Seawater density about 1,025 kg per cubic meter; fresh water about 1,000
as_written: about 1,025 kilograms per cubic meter, and fresh water about 1,000
source: NOAA / UNESCO seawater equation of state (TEOS-10)

text: Average ocean depth is about 3,700 meters
as_written: about 3,700 meters
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, ETOPO global relief model

text: A long wave in 3,700 m of water travels about 700 km/h (derived)
as_written: roughly 700 kilometers an hour
source: Shallow-water wave theory; NOAA tsunami speed explanation

text: Melting ice sheets cause sea level to fall near the ice sheet and rise more than average far away (gravitational fingerprint)
as_written: near a melting ice sheet, the sea level can actually fall
source: Mitrovica et al. 2001, Nature, 'Recent mass balance of polar ice sheets inferred from patterns of global sea-level change'

text: Melting floating ice barely changes sea level
as_written: When it melts, the level barely changes
source: Archimedes' principle; Noerdlinger and Brower 2007, Geophysical Journal International

text: Antarctic ice sheet sea-level equivalent is about 58 meters
as_written: about 58 meters
source: Bedmap2, Fretwell et al. 2013, The Cryosphere

text: Greenland ice sheet sea-level equivalent is about 7 meters
as_written: Greenland holds about 7 meters
source: BedMachine Greenland, Morlighem et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters (7.42 m)

text: Mountain glaciers hold roughly a third of a meter of sea-level equivalent
as_written: roughly a third of a meter
source: Farinotti et al. 2019, Nature Geoscience (about 0.32 m)

text: Total is about 66 meters; USGS rounds to about 70 meters
as_written: about 66 meters ... about 70
source: Sum of the sources above; US Geological Survey Water Science School

text: Dividing ice water by present ocean area gives slightly over 70 meters (derived)
as_written: a bit over 70 meters
source: Author's calculation using ocean area of about 361 million km2 (NOAA)

text: About four in ten people live within 100 km of a coast
as_written: About four in ten people on Earth live within 100 kilometers of a coast
source: United Nations Atlas of the Oceans

text: More than 600 million people live on land less than ten meters above sea level
as_written: More than 600 million live on land less than ten meters above the sea
source: McGranahan, Balk and Anderson 2007, Environment and Urbanization; IPCC AR6

text: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level
as_written: about a quarter of the country already sits below sea level
source: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) / Dutch government

text: Britton Hill, the highest point in Florida, is 105 meters
as_written: Britton Hill, the highest point in the state at 105 meters
source: US Geological Survey

text: Ice melt would add roughly two percent to ocean volume (derived: about 27 million km3 of water versus about 1.335 billion km3 ocean)
as_written: About two percent more water
source: NOAA ocean volume; ice volumes from sources above; author's calculation

text: Seawater is about 3.5 percent salt
as_written: about 3.5 percent salt
source: NOAA National Ocean Service

text: AMOC carries heat north and moderates Western Europe's climate
as_written: helps keep Western Europe milder
source: NOAA / Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution; IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 9

text: IPCC judges an abrupt AMOC collapse before 2100 unlikely, with low confidence beyond 2100; other studies suggest collapse could come sooner
as_written: an abrupt collapse before the year 2100 is unlikely
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group I (2021) Chapter 9; contrasting view in Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen 2023, Nature Communications

text: The Younger Dryas began about 12,900 years ago and is often linked to a meltwater pulse, a link still debated
as_written: about 12,900 years ago, called the Younger Dryas
source: Broecker et al. 1989, Nature; Carlson 2013 review, Quaternary Science Reviews

text: Glaciers and ice sheets cover about ten percent of Earth's land
as_written: Ice covers about ten percent of the land on Earth
source: US Geological Survey

text: Fresh snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of sunlight; open ocean reflects about 6 percent
as_written: eighty or ninety percent ... about six percent
source: US National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), albedo explanation

text: Greenland lost about 270 billion tonnes of ice per year since 2002, Antarctica about 150 billion tonnes per year
as_written: about 270 billion tonnes ... about 150 billion tonnes a year
source: NASA GRACE and GRACE-FO, NASA Global Climate Change Ice Sheets page

text: Greenland ice holds more than two quadrillion tonnes (about 2.9 million km3 x 917 kg/m3)
as_written: more than two quadrillion tonnes
source: BedMachine Greenland volume; author's calculation

text: At 270 billion tonnes per year, Greenland would take about ten thousand years to melt (derived)
as_written: about ten thousand years
source: Author's calculation from the figures above

text: Greenland runaway-loss threshold estimated between 0.8 and 3.2 C, best estimate 1.6 C above pre-industrial
as_written: between 0.8 and 3.2 degrees Celsius ... best guess of 1.6
source: Robinson, Calov and Ganopolski 2012, Nature Climate Change

text: Burning all reachable fossil fuels could eliminate the Antarctic ice sheet over millennia
as_written: burning all the fossil fuels we can reach could eliminate the whole ice sheet
source: Winkelmann et al. 2015, Science Advances

text: Thwaites Glacier is about the size of Florida and holds about 65 cm of sea-level equivalent
as_written: about the size of Florida ... about 65 centimeters
source: International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration (ITGC); NASA

text: Sea level during the last interglacial about 125,000 years ago was roughly five to ten meters higher; sources of the water are debated
as_written: about 125,000 years ago ... between five and ten meters higher
source: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 2 and Chapter 9; Dutton et al. 2015, Science

text: Mid-Pliocene about three million years ago had CO2 near modern levels and higher seas; estimates range widely
as_written: About three million years ago, in the mid-Pliocene
source: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 2; Dumitru et al. 2019, Nature; PRISM project, USGS

text: Antarctic ice sheet first formed about 34 million years ago
as_written: about 34 million years ago
source: Zachos et al. 2001, Science; Eocene-Oligocene transition

text: Arctic Ocean surface was around 23 C about 55 million years ago during the PETM
as_written: About 55 million years ago ... around 23 degrees Celsius
source: Sluijs et al. 2006, Nature (IODP Expedition 302, ACEX cores)

text: Eocene Arctic held swamp forests and alligator relatives on Ellesmere Island
as_written: swamp forests and relatives of alligators, on Ellesmere Island
source: Eberle and Greenwood 2012, Geological Society of America Bulletin; Canadian Museum of Nature

text: Atmospheric CO2 is above 420 parts per million
as_written: above 420 parts per million
source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa record

text: Deep ocean takes about a thousand years to turn over
as_written: about a thousand years to turn over
source: NOAA National Ocean Service / Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

text: Scandinavia is still rising at close to a centimeter a year after the last ice age
as_written: close to a centimeter a year
source: BIFROST GPS network, Milne et al. 2001, Science; Finnish Geospatial Research Institute

text: West Antarctic bedrock is rising up to 41 mm per year
as_written: up to 41 millimeters a year
source: Barletta et al. 2018, Science

text: Iceland's eruption rates were 30 to 50 times higher after deglaciation about 12,000 years ago
as_written: somewhere between 30 and 50 times higher
source: Maclennan et al. 2002, Geochemistry Geophysics Geosystems; Sigmundsson et al. 2010, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society

text: Global eruption rates were two to six times higher after the last ice age
as_written: two to six times more frequent
source: Huybers and Langmuir 2009, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

text: University of Edinburgh team found 91 new volcanoes under West Antarctica, bringing the total to 138
as_written: 91 previously unknown volcanoes ... 138
source: van Wyk de Vries et al. 2017, Geological Society of London Special Publications

text: Ice melt has delayed the next negative leap second by about three years
as_written: delayed the next negative leap second by about three years
source: Agnew 2024, Nature, 'A global timekeeping problem postponed by global warming'
